When you work with APIs, you are essentially asking another program to share data or perform actions for you. This exchange happens through HTTP requests, usually GET to fetch data or POST to send new information. Most modern APIs return data in JSON format, which is easy for both humans and computers to read.

Before making requests, you often need authentication—typically an API key—to prove you have permission. Once you start, you must respect rate limits, which prevent you from sending too many requests in a short time. If you ignore them, the API might block you temporarily. Finally, always include error handling in your code. Networks fail, servers go down, or you might send bad data. By checking response codes like 404 or 500, you can respond gracefully instead of crashing. These basics will help you build reliable integrations.
